title: What is Parquet — a file format that stores data in columns instead of rows, which is much faster for analytics queries because you only read the columns you need (like reading only the "salary" column from a table with 100 columns).

s1_definition.profdef: Apache Parquet is an open-source columnar storage file format optimized for analytical workloads. Instead of storing data row by row, it stores values column by column, which lets a query read only the columns it needs (column pruning), skip irrelevant data using column statistics (predicate pushdown), and compress each column very efficiently because similar values sit together. It is the de facto storage format for data lakes and big-data engines like Spark.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India keeps a giant ledger with a hundred columns per transaction: account id, amount, timestamp, branch, device, and ninety-six more. A row-based file is like a book where each page holds one complete transaction with all hundred fields, so to total just the "amount" column you must flip through every page reading all hundred fields. Parquet is like re-filing the ledger so all the amounts sit together in one slim folder, all the branches in another. Now to total amounts you grab just the amount folder and ignore the other ninety-nine — far less reading, and since all amounts look alike they squash down tiny when zipped.
s1_definition.oneliner: Parquet stores data by column so analytics reads only the columns it needs, skips irrelevant data, and compresses far better than row formats.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Apache Parquet is an open-source columnar storage file format optimized for analytical workloads. Instead of storing data row by row, it stores values column by column, which lets a query read only the columns it needs (column pruning), skip irrelevant data using column statistics (predicate pushdown), and compress each column very efficiently because similar values sit together. It is the de facto storage format for data lakes and big-data engines like Spark.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India keeps a giant ledger with a hundred columns per transaction: account id, amount, timestamp, branch, device, and ninety-six more. A row-based file is like a book where each page holds one complete transaction with all hundred fields, so to total just the "amount" column you must flip through every page reading all hundred fields. Parquet is like re-filing the ledger so all the amounts sit together in one slim folder, all the branches in another. Now to total amounts you grab just the amount folder and ignore the other ninety-nine — far less reading, and since all amounts look alike they squash down tiny when zipped.

**One line to remember:** Parquet stores data by column so analytics reads only the columns it needs, skips irrelevant data, and compresses far better than row formats.

sections.s2_technical:
The fundamental idea is columnar layout. A row-oriented format like CSV or a typical OLTP page stores all fields of row 1, then all fields of row 2. Parquet flips this: it stores all values of column A together, then all of column B. The immediate payoff for analytics is column pruning. If a query is `SELECT SUM(amount) FROM transactions`, Parquet reads only the amount column's bytes and never touches the other ninety-nine columns, which can cut I/O by orders of magnitude.

The second payoff is predicate pushdown via statistics. Parquet organizes data into row groups, and within each row group each column chunk stores metadata including the minimum and maximum values. If a query filters `WHERE txn_date = '2024-10-29'` and a row group's max date is '2024-09-30', the engine skips that entire row group without decoding it. Combined with partitioning the files on disk by date, scans prune enormous amounts of data before reading it.

The third payoff is compression and encoding. Because a column holds values of the same type and often with repetition — many transactions share the same branch code or currency — Parquet applies encodings like dictionary encoding and run-length encoding, then a codec like Snappy or Zstandard. Similar values next to each other compress dramatically better than mixed-type rows, which saves storage cost and further reduces bytes read.

Parquet is self-describing: the file footer holds the full schema and the statistics, so engines read the footer first to plan the scan. It supports nested and complex types, and it integrates natively with Spark, Hive, Presto/Trino, and cloud warehouses. A senior nuance is that Parquet is designed for write-once, read-many analytical use, not for frequent single-row updates, which is why it pairs with lake table formats like Delta Lake and Iceberg that add ACID transactions and updates on top of Parquet files. The trade-off versus row formats is that Parquet is excellent for wide scans and aggregations but poor for retrieving one whole row with all columns, which is where a row store or OLTP database still wins. In a bank, storing transaction history in partitioned Parquet makes analytical queries like per-branch quarterly totals both cheap and fast.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores transactions with many columns, but a report only needs the amount. Reading all columns wastes huge I/O. This is exactly columnar storage with column pruning — read only the amount column.

Problem 2 — A report only wants one date's data, but the file holds a year. This is exactly predicate pushdown using min/max statistics — skip row groups that cannot match.

Problem 3 — Storage is expensive and amounts repeat. This is exactly columnar compression — like values stored together compress far better.

To run anywhere without a Parquet library, the mini-project simulates Parquet's model in Java. `Transaction` is a wide record. `RowStore` holds records row by row and must scan everything. `ColumnStore` holds each column separately, tracks per-column min/max statistics for pushdown, and can sum the amount column reading only that column. The demo loads the same transactions into both and shows the column store reading far fewer "cells" and skipping a non-matching row group.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four transactions, each with four columns (txn id, account id, amount, date), all on 2024-10-29.

Step 1 — Load both stores. The row store keeps four complete rows. The column store splits the data into an amount column and a date column and records min and max date statistics, both equal to 2024-10-29.

Step 2 — Sum amount in the row store. To total the amount column, the row store must walk every row and read all four fields of each, counting sixteen cells read even though only four were needed.

Step 3 — Sum amount in the column store. The column store reads only the amount column, touching four cells. Same total, but a quarter of the I/O because the other three columns were pruned.

Step 4 — Predicate pushdown query. A query asks for the amount total on 2023-01-01. The column store checks its row-group statistics, sees the target date is before the minimum date, and skips the entire row group without reading a single value.

Step 5 — Output. Both stores return the same amount total of 9500, but the column store read far fewer cells, and the pushdown query returned zero while reading nothing at all. This is why analytics on wide tables is vastly cheaper in Parquet.

```
INFO: === SUM(amount) — same answer, very different I/O ===
INFO: ROW store summed amount, cells read = 16
INFO: Row total   = 9500.00
INFO: COLUMN store summed amount, cells read = 4
INFO: Column total= 9500.00
INFO: === Predicate pushdown for a non-matching date ===
INFO: PUSHDOWN: skipped row group (target 2023-01-01 outside [2024-10-29,2024-10-29]) — 0 cells read
INFO: Result = 0
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Apache Parquet is an open-source columnar storage file format built for analytics. Instead of storing data row by row, it stores values column by column, and that one change unlocks three big wins. The first is column pruning: a query that only needs the amount reads just the amount column's bytes and never touches the other columns, which can cut I/O by orders of magnitude on a wide table. The second is predicate pushdown: Parquet groups data into row groups, and each column chunk stores min and max statistics, so a query filtering on a date can skip entire row groups that cannot possibly match, especially when the files are also partitioned by date on disk. The third is compression: because a column holds values of the same type and often repeats, encodings like dictionary and run-length plus a codec like Snappy or Zstandard shrink the data dramatically.

Parquet is self-describing, with a footer holding the schema and statistics, which is why engines read the footer first to plan the scan, and it integrates natively with Spark, Trino, Hive, and cloud warehouses. A senior point I always add is that Parquet is designed for write-once, read-many analytical use, not frequent single-row updates, which is why it pairs with lake table formats like Delta Lake and Iceberg that add ACID transactions and updates on top of Parquet files. The trade-off is that it is excellent for wide scans and aggregations but poor at fetching one entire row with all its columns, where a row store still wins.

In my project at the National Bank of India we stored transaction history in partitioned Parquet in the data lake. A report that just needed total amounts read only the amount column and ignored the dozens of other columns, and a report scoped to one date skipped every row group outside that date using the min and max statistics. The result was that analytical queries like per-branch quarterly totals were both far cheaper in storage and far faster to run than they would have been in a row format, which is exactly why Parquet is the default storage format for a bank's analytics lake.

keyPoints: Parquet: columnar, compressed, schema — best for analytics
Avro: row-based, schema evolution, compact — best for Kafka
ORC: columnar, optimized for Hive — similar to Parquet
Choose: Parquet for reads (analytics), Avro for writes (streaming)
